questions.q: In the Thornfield Analytics script, how does the script decide which VMs to stop or start?
options: It acts on every VM in the subscription, with no filtering at all
It only acts on VMs created in the last 24 hours
It asks the user to type each VM name manually every time it runs
It filters VMs on a tag (AutoShutdown = true) instead of relying on a hardcoded list of VM names
questions.explain: Tag-based targeting means the script automatically stays correct as VMs are added or removed, instead of requiring a maintained exception list.

questions.q: Why does the script call Get-AzVM -Status and check the VM's current power state before calling Stop-AzVM or Start-AzVM?
options: Because checking status is faster than just stopping the VM directly
Because Stop-AzVM requires the status to be checked first or it will not run at all
Because that's what makes the script idempotent — it only acts when the current state doesn't already match the desired one
It's not necessary — the check is only there for logging purposes
questions.explain: Chapter 1's idempotency principle: a script safe to rerun checks current state first, so running it repeatedly does nothing extra once the goal state is reached.

questions.q: What would happen if this script skipped the try/catch and continue around each VM's logic, and VM number 7 out of 40 threw an error?
options: The whole script would stop, and VMs 8 through 40 would never get evaluated
Nothing — PowerShell automatically skips failed VMs without any error handling
Only VM 7 would be affected; the rest would still run exactly the same way
The script would automatically retry VM 7 three times before continuing
questions.explain: Without the try/catch/continue pattern, an unhandled error in a loop halts the entire run, leaving every later item unprocessed.

questions.q: Why is -ErrorAction Stop added to the Stop-AzVM call inside the try block?
options: It prevents the VM from actually being stopped, for safety
It is required syntax for every Az module cmdlet
It stops the entire script immediately on any error, everywhere
It forces the cmdlet to throw a catchable exception instead of writing a non-terminating error that the catch block would otherwise miss
questions.explain: Many Az cmdlets write non-terminating errors by default; -ErrorAction Stop converts that into a terminating exception that try/catch can actually respond to.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how does this script actually get run on a schedule in production, rather than someone running it manually from their laptop?
options: It becomes an Azure Automation Runbook, triggered by a schedule resource with no human involved
It runs only when a VM is manually restarted
A human has to remember to run it every evening and morning
It is triggered by an email reminder sent to the on-call engineer
questions.explain: Chapter 2's Azure Automation approach is what actually puts a script like this into unattended production use, scheduled rather than run by hand.
